source.title: Memory for goals: an activation-based model

confidence_rationale: A formal, empirically-fit computational model of exactly the phenomenon MECH-524 needs to license: a suspended goal is not erased but decays in activation and is recoverable via priming, tested against latency/error data from a task (Tower of Hanoi) that is architecturally about suspension and resumption of subgoals. Directly grounds the preserve-don't-erase framing and the need for an explicit re-priming trigger rather than passive persistence.
failure_signatures: A suspended goal's activation decays with elapsed time and with interference from intervening goals -- so a parked goal left un-reprimed for long enough, or heavily interleaved with unrelated activity, becomes progressively harder to retrieve even though its representation was never deleted. Passive persistence alone (SD-039's trace surviving) is not sufficient for reliable resumption at arbitrary delay; an explicit reactivation/priming event is load-bearing.

The model's priming constraint predicts that resumption quality depends on the availability of the right retrieval cues at the moment capacity returns -- an interruption_snapshot with no cue-bearing content (or a re-seeding trigger that does not supply the snapshot as a cue) would fail to accelerate retrieval even if the trace is intact.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Suspended goals are represented via the general memory constructs of activation and associative priming rather than a specialized goal-stack structure. Three constraints govern behavior: (1) interference -- residual activation from old, already-resolved goals competes with and slows retrieval of the currently relevant one; (2) strengthening -- the more thoroughly a goal is encoded before suspension, the more durable its later retrieval; (3) priming -- appropriate retrieval cues at the moment of resumption reactivate a pending goal's activation, counteracting the decay it underwent while suspended. Fit against latency and error data from Tower of Hanoi, a puzzle that requires continual suspension and resumption of subgoals.
mapping.ree_translation: Directly grounds two design choices in MECH-524. First, preserve-don't-erase: a parked goal's representation persists (paralleling SD-039's un-erased trace) but its retrievability decays with time and competing activity, so re-elevating a parked slot cannot be a bare presence check -- it needs a strength/decay term. Second, and more specifically, it grounds why the mechanism proposes an explicit re-seeding trigger (spare-compute signal or sleep entry pushing the interruption_snapshot into MECH-293/MECH-285) rather than relying on the parked goal to simply 'still be there': Altmann & Trafton's priming constraint says resumption is cue-driven, and the interruption_snapshot is precisely the cue payload the trigger delivers.
mapping.mapping_caveat: ACT-R production-system / goal-stack cognitive architecture fit to a discrete symbolic puzzle domain (Tower of Hanoi), not a continuous world-model / latent-state RL substrate; 'activation' here is a scalar memory-strength construct, not literally z_world/z_self/z_goal. The three constraints are architecturally suggestive, not a mechanistic proof that REE's snapshot payload needs to include CEM stage or rule-arbitration weights specifically -- that richer payload is a REE-side design extension beyond what this paper tests.
mapping.source_context: Formal computational model (ACT-R framework) fit to human latency and error data from Tower of Hanoi performance, a classic means-ends puzzle requiring repeated suspension and resumption of subgoals under working-memory load.

confidence_components.notes: Strong source: a canonical, well-cited, empirically-fit computational model built for exactly this phenomenon class. Mapping fidelity good at the structural level (decay + cue-driven reactivation of a suspended goal) but the substrate (symbolic production system vs. REE's latent world-model) is different enough that specific numeric predictions do not transfer, only the qualitative architecture.
